title: Facing Off Against Kramnik and WINNING!! | Titled Tuesday | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: d4, and the knight to f6 — Black declines to fight for the centre with a pawn, planning to let White build it and then strike back. The makings of a King's Indian.
The knight to c3, the classical set-up — White is happy to take the whole centre and dare Black to challenge it.
d6 — the King's Indian in earnest. Black cedes space on purpose, banking on a later …e5 or …c5 break to hit the centre from the side.
e4, and White has the broad pawn centre the opening invites. The whole game is now a question: can Black crack it before White uses it?
g6, preparing the fianchetto — the dark-squared bishop is the soul of this defence, and it belongs on the long diagonal aiming straight through the centre at White's queenside.
The bishop to e2, a calm, classical developing square.
The bishop settles on g7 and White brings the knight to f3 — both sides just developing, the tension still coiled.
Black castles, tucking the king behind the fianchetto — one of the safest shelters in all of chess.
White castles too. A textbook classical King's Indian; now the plans diverge — White expands, Black looks for a break.
The bishop to g4, pinning the f3-knight. Black would love to trade it off, because that knight is the natural defender of White's centre.
The bishop to e3, developing and eyeing the dark squares.
The knight to c6, piling a second attacker onto d4 and White's centre.
d5 — White answers the pressure by pushing past, grabbing space and kicking the knight. This is the main King's Indian tension: a big White pawn chain versus Black's piece pressure.
The bishop takes on f3 and White recaptures with the bishop — Black cashes in the pin, trading off a key defender of the light squares.
The knight swings to e5, the classic King's Indian outpost, and White retreats the bishop to e2 to keep it. A beautiful square: central, secure, hard to dislodge.
c6 — the thematic break. Black chips at the base of White's pawn chain to open lines on the queenside.
a4 — White grabs queenside space of its own and takes b5 away from Black. The two sides are now racing on opposite wings.
The tension resolves on d5 — the pawns come off and the position opens a touch, both recaptures the engine's top choice.
The knight reroutes toward d7, unclogging and eyeing c5 and e5. Still all main-road stuff; the engine can't separate the sides.
a5, clamping down — White fixes the queenside and cramps Black's play there.
a6, shoring up b5 and keeping the structure intact.

The bishop to d4, offering to trade the dark-squared bishops. It's a slight concession — the engine would rather reroute the knight to a4 — but trading Black's proud g7-bishop is a reasonable positional aim.
The rook comes to c8, onto the half-open c-file — the natural home for a King's Indian rook once the c-file opens.
The queen to d2, connecting the rooks and supporting the dark-squared plans.
The knight to c5, a strong central post eyeing the queenside light squares.
The bishop to f3, defending the centre and reinforcing d5. The position is balanced and rich — both sides fully developed, no weaknesses yet.

And here's the slip. It was the c-knight that wanted to reroute to d7; instead the f6-knight drops back, and the g7-bishop is left to its fate. Bishop takes g7, the roof comes off, and then b4 rounds up the loose knight on c5 — a whole piece, and the needle swings past three points to White. Send the other knight to d7 and none of this is on the board.
White pounces the way the engine demands: the bishop takes on g7, stripping away the fianchetto — and the follow-up b4 will hit the loose knight. White is suddenly winning.

The king has to do the recapturing — leave the bishop on g7 and it takes the f8-rook next, so there's no choice. Kxg7, and the dark squares around the king are permanently tender now; White is one pawn-thrust from collecting the loose knight.

But the favour is returned. b4 was the kill — the pawn hits the knight on c5, and once it's taken the piece simply falls. Instead the rook swings to e1, the win evaporates, and the eval more than halves. A blitz game between two very fast players; the advantage sloshes back and forth.
Black seizes the reprieve — the knight back to f6, re-covering the light squares and climbing back to level. Crisis survived.
The queen to d4, centralising and pressuring the dark squares.
The knight to d7, calmly holding everything together.
The bishop drops to e2, a quiet regroup.
The queen to c7, eyeing the open c-file and the loose queenside.
The bishop to f1 — passive, the engine would rather reroute more actively, but the position is roughly balanced.
The rooks come to e8, contesting the centre file.
h3, a useful little luft, taking g4 away from Black's pieces.
The queen to c5, offering to trade queens into a comfortable position.
The queen to d2, sidestepping the trade for now.
The knight returns to e5 — that outpost again, the heart of Black's play.
The rook to a4, defending along the fourth rank and keeping an eye on the queenside.
h5, grabbing a little kingside space — slightly loosening, but the position stays roughly level.
The king to h1, a prudent tuck out of any back-rank or diagonal ideas.
e6 — Black strikes at the centre, prying open lines against White's slightly awkward pieces.
White takes on e6 — but the engine calls it an error; a quiet move like f4 was stronger, and now Black's rooks come alive on the open file.
The rook recaptures on e6, seizing the file.
The rook to d1 — again the engine prefers f4; White keeps missing the most testing continuation as the clock bites.
The rooks double on the e-file — Black is building real pressure down the centre now.
The queen to d4, trying to hold the fort — but it's an inaccuracy; the engine wanted to force matters instead.
The knight to c6, hitting the queen and gaining a tempo for the coming break.
The queen to d2 — and now the eval tips to Black. Small errors have accumulated, and White's position is quietly worse.
d5 — Black plants the pawn in the centre and takes over. This is the payoff of all that pressure: a mobile centre against a passive White army.
The bishop to d3, trying to blunt the coming push.
The pawn storms on to d4 and the knight is driven to e2 — Black's centre knifes forward, and it's Black firmly in control now, on the board and on the clock.
